summary: Locations on Earth analogous to those on the Moon and Mars are used to simulate testing and training but are selected based on field experience with no defined way to compare. This report covers the development of the Earth Analog Atlas, an interactive map that scores every land area on Earth based on how analogous they are to the Moon and Mars. The Earth was broken up into 89,011 cells of 0.5°. Each cell received a weighted score based on nine criteria, including bare ground, dryness, cold, roughness, elevation, remoteness, rusty and grey colours and polar light derived from open source climate, vegetation, elevation and image data. The known analog sites were scored using the same method. Analogous environments performed well, with the McMurdo Dry Valleys being in the top 1% of land areas on Earth for the Moon and the Atacama Desert being within the top 21% for Mars. Analogues selected primarily for geological training performed poorly, showing that this index scores environments, not geological types. Using this method, new potential analogues for Mars were the high Andes and Tibetan Plateau and new potential analogues for the Moon were the ice free terrain of the High Arctic in Canada and Greenland. We can see that a transparent global similarity index can recreate field practice and show potential new analogues. However, to make this method complete, a separate geological score and target data for each planet is required.
details:
1. Introduction

This report addresses the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars. Teams are tasked to identify and characterise new terrestrial analogues using open data. This should be presented in the form of a map, visualisation or other tool.

Currently analogues such as Devon Island, the Atacama Desert and Arizona lava fields are used to simulate testing and training. These are often selected based on field experience and characterised individually. However, there is no standardised way to compare terrestrial landscapes to planetary surfaces, making it difficult to find new or complementary analogues over large areas.

Our aims are:

  1. Quantify: Convert ‘Moon-like’ and ‘Mars-like’ into quantifiable criteria that can be calculated for any location on Earth.
  2. Validate: Ensure that established analogues receive a high score, validating our method.
  3. Discover and explain: Rank locations not currently used as analogues and show why they are analogous.

2. Methodology

2.1 Concept and design rationale

The concept was to create a single similarity index that could be calculated for any location on Earth. We made some considerations when designing:

Global score: By scoring all land areas we can ensure that we are not just confirming what is already known. This means we can discover locations that have not been suggested.

Transparent and adjustable scoring: All criteria were normalised between 0-1 and then combined using a weighted mean. This means that the score can be easily traced back to its inputs. The weighting was done using sliders as different analogues were needed depending on the reason for testing (rover traverse vs crew isolation).

Separate surface, subsurface and operational analogues: Surface criteria were taken from satellite data. However, subsurface areas such as caves, lava tubes and underwater habitats cannot be seen from orbit. These are still important for base concepts (lava tubes are potential shelters on both the Moon and Mars), so we have separated them into a different category (Caves & underwater).

Open source validation: Known analogues were plotted onto the map with their scores. Anyone judging or using the tool can instantly see where our method matches field experience.

The tool was designed using a game-like format. This gave the tool a clean, easy to understand layout for students and the general public. The map acts as your playing board, the cards on the right provide character information for the analogue, the sliders are used to adjust the weighting and new discoveries are displayed using a loot list.

2.2 Working process

We went through six steps and ensured that we reviewed each step.

  1. Challenge Breakdown: We read through the brief and identified key words: new (we must go beyond providing known analogues) and characterise (we must provide a numerical reason why each is an analogue). We then researched existing analogue programmes and found that there was no standardised way to quantify.
  2. Criteria Selection: We converted lunar and Martian surface characteristics into quantifiable terrestrial criteria. We improved initial criteria (elevation, temperature and soil type) into more meaningful criteria (roughness instead of elevation) and included criteria that would be strong initial filters (lack of vegetation and dryness). We also included remoteness and polar light as these are important for a lunar south pole base.
  3. Cave and Underwater Consideration: We felt that these were relevant for operational analogues but cannot be seen from orbit, so we have included them as a separate layer of known analogues. This will be developed in the future as a data driven subsurface layer.
  4. Data Collection & Processing: We researched open source data globally for climate, vegetation, elevation, imagery, climate zones and population centres. We then resampled this data to create a uniform 0.5° grid. Each criterion was normalised to between 0-1. We also spot checked the values for known locations.
  5. Scoring & Validation: We calculated scores for Mars and the Moon for all cells and known analogues. We then validated by looking at where the known analogues ranked. This showed us that the index scores based on the environment, not geological factors (Section 4.1).
  6. Tool Development: We created our interactive atlas. We started by creating a game-like map with 21 known analogues. We then added a global heat map, live weighting and automatic discovery of new analogues. Finally we added the ability to scan a point with a satellite image preview.

2.3 Data sources

The current version uses six open source global datasets. These were resampled to create the 0.5° grid.

Table 1: Current version of tool uses:

  • WorldClim 2.1 (WorldClim, academic; 10′): Annual mean temperature, annual precipitation
  • Global Land NDVI (Copernicus, EU; 5 km): Vegetation cover: long-term mean for 21 June, 1999–2017
  • ETOPO1 (NOAA; 1′, used at 0.5°): Elevation and local relief
  • Blue Marble Next Generation (NASA; ~4 km per pixel as used): Surface colour; satellite preview in the atlas
  • Köppen-Geiger climate zones (Rubel et al.; 0.5°): Climate class; ice-sheet exclusion
  • GeoNames (GeoNames; point data): Distance to the nearest city of 15,000+ people

For known analogues we sampled the same layers using their coordinates. Locations were taken from published programme descriptions (see references).

2.4 Scoring model

Every land cell is given a score between 0-1 for each target body. This score is calculated using a weighted mean of the normalised criteria.

Grid: The analysis grid was 0.5° x 0.5° cells. This is approximately 55 km at the equator. There are 89,011 land cells.

Criteria: Each criterion was scaled between 0-1, with 1 being most planet like.

Table 2: Scoring criteria and default weighting (Mars weight / Moon weight):

  • Bare ground (Low NDVI): 2 / 2
  • Dryness (Low annual precipitation): 2 / 1.5
  • Cold (Low mean annual temperature): 1.5 / 1
  • Rugged terrain (Elevation spread within the cell’s neighbourhood): 1 / 1.5
  • Altitude (Elevation: thin air, high UV): 1 / –
  • Isolation (Distance to the nearest city): 1 / 1.5
  • Rusty surface (Red-brown surface colour): 1.5 / –
  • Grey surface (Grey, unsaturated surface colour): – / 1.5
  • Polar light (Low sun angle at high latitude, as at the lunar south pole): – / 1

Score. For a cell and target body with weights wᵢ:
S = Σ wᵢsᵢ / Σ wᵢ

If there is no data for a criterion it is not included in either the numerator or the denominator. This means that a missing layer will not affect the score. The weights are default but can be changed by the user. The scores will update automatically.

New Discoveries: All cells are ranked based on the target body selected. The top 8 cells with a minimum distance of 300 km from any known analogue are suggested. By default any cells with a climate class of ice cap (Köppen EF) are excluded as they score high for being cold, bare and remote but are not useful for terrain analogues.

2.5 The interactive tool: Earth Analog Atlas

The tool is a single page website. It contains a global map (created using D3 with Natural Earth Projection) and all of the grid and analogue data embedded. The tool contains six main functions:

  • Heat Map: All land on Earth is coloured based on how analogous it is to Mars or the Moon. Toggle between the two planets. Includes a colour gradient legend.
  • Analogue Markers and Cards: The 21 known analogues are separated into categories (Moon, Mars, Caves & Underwater and Verification). Hovering over a marker will zoom in and display the card. The card displays the location, coordinates, what programme uses it, what makes it an analogue, and bars to show how analogous it is to the Moon and Mars. It also contains a breakdown of the score for each criterion along with raw data (Temperature, Precipitation, NDVI, Elevation, Climate Zone and Distance to nearest city).
  • Point Scan: Hovering over any point will lock onto the 55 km cell and display the card for that cell, or ‘Open Ocean’ if it is over water.
  • Satellite Preview: Each card has a cropped satellite view (8°) using NASA Blue Marble. The cell is highlighted in the centre.
  • Live Weighting: Sliders for each criterion so all scores can be recalculated. The heat map and new discoveries list will instantly update. Options to toggle the heat map and exclude ice sheets.
  • New Discoveries: The top 8 new discoveries based on the target body.

Clicking on a discovery will zoom to that location. A ‘Discovered’ progress bar fills as the user views analogues. This adds a gaming aspect encouraging exploration. Filters can be used to show/hide the categories. The map can be zoomed and panned.

3. Results

3.1 Validation against known analogs

This method matches field practice for environmental analogues. The McMurdo Dry Valleys perform well, scoring highest for Moon analogues (82%, top 1% of land). Concordia, McMurdo and the Atacama Desert all score within the top 21% for Mars. The sites are split into three groups. The field environment analogues score within the top 20% to top 52%. The six geological training analogues score below the median land cell, with Meteor Crater scoring top 52% and Nördlinger Ries scoring top 94%. The habitat and isolation analogues score throughout the range, with Concordia scoring top 13% and LunAres scoring top 82%, as they do not rely on the surrounding landscape.

Calculated using the atlas grid and analogue data. Default weights. 20 sites with land data (Aquarius is offshore).

3.2 New candidate analogs

Using the default weights, the strongest new Mars analogues are clustered in two high altitude cold desert areas, the central Andes and Tibetan Plateau. The strongest new Moon analogues are within the ice free High Arctic terrain of Canada and Greenland. All eight Mars analogues scored higher than any known Mars analogues. Only the McMurdo Dry Valleys (82%) score within the range of the new analogues (78-87%).

Table 3: Top new analogue scores (Default weights, No ice caps, Minimum distance from known analogues):

  • Mars: −28.25, −69.25, High Andes, Chile/Argentina (Puna), 72%
  • Mars: −22.25, −67.75, Altiplano, Bolivia/Chile, 70%
  • Mars: 36.25, 84.25, Kunlun / northern Tibetan Plateau, 70%
  • Mars: 34.25, 80.25, Western Tibetan Plateau, 69%
  • Mars: 30.25, 85.75, Southern Tibetan Plateau, 68%
  • Mars: 36.75, 92.25, Qaidam Basin margin, China, 67%
  • Mars: 39.75, 92.25, Kumtag Desert area, China, 67%
  • Mars: 36.25, 77.75, Karakoram–Kunlun, 67%
  • Moon: 81.75, −72.25, Ellesmere Island, Canada, 87%
  • Moon: 79.25, −90.75, Axel Heiberg / Ellesmere, Canada, 87%
  • Moon: 78.75, −67.75, NW Greenland, 83%
  • Moon: 77.25, −81.25, Ellesmere Island, Canada, 81%
  • Moon: 76.25, −61.25, NW Greenland, 81%
  • Moon: 72.25, −53.25, W Greenland, 80%
  • Moon: 80.25, −20.75, NE Greenland, 79%
  • Moon: 82.25, −49.75, N Greenland, 78%

4. Analysis and discussion

4.1 Interpreting the validation

Low rankings give us useful information. Nördlinger Ries, Sudbury, Meteor Crater, Lanzarote and Río Tinto are all used for impact geology, volcanology or mineral studies for different reasons. Ries, Sudbury and Río Tinto are all located in temperate areas with lots of vegetation (NDVI between 0.49-0.80). Meteor Crater and Lanzarote are both dry, however they are warm, close to towns (60 km and 9 km away) and the size of the crater/lava fields is too small to improve the score for roughness in a 55 km cell. Therefore they only score around the median. As this score is based on environment they are penalised correctly and a separate geological score needs to be created (Section 5.1). Enclosed habitats and caves (LunAres, Sardinia caves, Lofthellir lava tubes) are operational analogues and do not aim to have a similar environment to other planets.

There are two things to consider when interpreting the map. Firstly, around 10% of land scores above 66% for Mars. This is largely due to ice sheets, so ice caps were excluded from new discoveries. Secondly, the median land cell scores 36% for Mars and 33% for the Moon, meaning anything over roughly 60% is unique.

4.2 Interpreting the new candidates

The region names are approximate and should be checked on a map for use in the field. The Puna and Qaidam Basin have already been mentioned in Mars analogue research, which validates our method. However, the other analogues have yet to be checked against the literature. The Moon analogues are biased to the Arctic as the polar light criterion rewards high latitudes. This is intentional as we want to find analogues to a south pole base.

4.3 Local case: Troodos Massif, Cyprus

We added the Troodos Massif as a verification analogue due to its ophiolite. This is oceanic crust and altered volcanic rock. Due to it being a vegetated temperate area it scores low (19% Mars, 7% Moon). Any value it has is geological, which the current index does not take into consideration (see Section 4.4).

4.4 Limitations

This is a regional environmental filter and should not be used in place of geological assessments.

  • Environmental not geological: Criteria are based on climate, vegetation, terrain and colour. Impact structures, basalt, ophiolite and specific minerals are not measured. This is why geological analogues like Ries, Sudbury and Troodos score low.
  • General comparison: Scores compare Earth to ‘the Moon’ and ‘Mars’. They do not compare to specific base areas such as lunar south pole regions or Jezero Crater. No planetary data has been used.
  • Low resolution: Each cell is 55 km, meaning small features would not be visible. HI-SEAS will only register around 963 m of elevation compared to its real ~2,500 m. Lanzarote will not register due to its size.
  • Seasonal vegetation: The NDVI layer is an average for 21 June. This means locations in the northern hemisphere will look greener and locations in the southern hemisphere will look more barren than the annual average. The southern analogues (Puna and Altiplano) may therefore score slightly higher and northern analogues slightly lower. This issue can be overcome by using an annual mean or maximum NDVI.
  • Ice sheets: Ice caps will score highly for being cold, bare and remote. They are excluded from new discoveries but will still affect the heat map. As the climate classes are assigned using 0.5° cells, this removes any ice free terrain within EF cells. This means the McMurdo Dry Valleys are classed as EF. This may therefore miss some valid polar analogues.
  • Most data is not from NASA: Only Blue Marble is from NASA.
  • Not detecting subsurface: Caves, lava tubes and underwater areas are only shown as known locations.

5. Conclusions

We wanted to see if we could discover and explain planetary analogues using a single transparent similarity index that can be calculated the same way for any location on Earth. The results indicate that this can work for environmental analogues.

  • A transparent similarity index can recreate field practice for environmental analogues. The McMurdo Dry Valleys are within the top 1% of land for Moon analogues. Concordia, McMurdo and the Atacama Desert are within the top 21% for Mars analogues. These analogues have scored well due to being cold, dry, bare and remote.
  • This does not account for geological analogues, as expected. Nördlinger Ries, Sudbury, Río Tinto and Troodos all score within the bottom 20%. Their value lies in impact structures, minerals or ophiolite rock. None of the nine criteria measure these. This is due to the scope of the model, not any issues with the data.
  • This does help to find new potential analogue regions. All eight new Mars analogues (central Andes, Tibetan Plateau) scored higher than any known Mars analogues. The new Moon analogues are in ice free High Arctic terrain. Some of these regions have already been mentioned in the analogue literature, validating the results. The remaining analogues need to be checked.
  • The data used has a low resolution. This means we are not getting precise scores. Each cell is 55 km, so the scores relate to regions, not individual field sites. Small sites like Lanzarote will not register.

Overall, the atlas converts an experience based selection into something repeatable and explorable. It is most useful as a first filter to show mission planners and researchers where to look.

5.1 Ways to improve

The scoring method remains the same. We would improve the data and targets. In order of importance:

  1. Use NASA Earth data: Use NASADEM or SRTM (30 m) for elevation and roughness, MODIS NDVI or HLS for vegetation, NASA POWER or MODIS for climate (land surface temperature) and VIIRS Black Marble for remoteness. This will also improve resolution to well below 55 km.
  2. Specific targets for sites: Create targeted profiles for named base/landing regions. For example, the lunar south pole would use LRO Diviner temperature and LOLA topography. Sites on Mars like Jezero would use MOLA, THEMIS and TES. This will answer the question ‘What are the most similar locations on Earth to this site?’
  3. Separate geological score: Include EMIT surface mineralogy for arid areas on Earth. Compare with CRISM mineral mapping on Mars. Also include impact structure and volcanic field layers. This will allow us to see how similar they are both geologically and environmentally. This will help with the Ries/Sudbury/Troodos case.
  4. Polar elevation: SRTM does not go beyond 60°N. We would use Copernicus GLO-30, ArcticDEM and REMA to cover the most important polar analogues for a south pole base.
  5. Practicality score: Show how accessible the site is (roads, airports) alongside similarity. This will show how practical it is to use the best analogue vs the most accessible.
  6. Subsurface layer: Include volcanic field maps, lava tube databases and karst maps (WOKAM). Flag any areas overlapping high scoring surface terrain. This will highlight any candidates for a full base analogue (surface EVA terrain + sheltered habitat site).
